transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-09-21 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52m
Attendees: James Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Moreno (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (SummitPay Product), Ethan Zhang (SummitPay CTO), Liam O'Connor (SummitPay SRE), Anika Patel (SummitPay Legal)

Summary:
Quick product walkthrough focusing on structured output (JSON mode), function/tool calling, and guardrails. Customer wants deterministic JSON output for downstream billing pipeline and to invoke internal tools (refunds, chargebacks) via function calls. Security and data residency questions (KMS, VPC) discussed. Agreed next steps to share security pack and pricing, and scope a pilot.

Topics covered:
- Redwood API structured output / JSON mode and schemas
- Function calling / tool integration patterns and Console demo
- Guardrails, validation, and failure modes (schema enforcement, fallback)
- Hosting options: Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC)
- Security: SOC 2, KMS/HSM, SAML/SSO, audit logs, RBAC

Transcript body:
[00:00] James: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about 50 minutes. quick intros?
[00:08] Maya: maya here, head of product at SummitPay, we'll mostly be looking at billing and dispute flows.
[00:12] Ethan: ethan, CTO, I'll be mostly listening for architecture and security.
[00:16] Liam: liam, on SRE, we'll look at latency and throughput constraints.
[00:20] Anika: anika from legal, quick Qs on data retention and audit logs.
[00:25] James: perfect. priya and alex from our side will run the demo \u0004 priya will do the JSON structured-output flow, alex will show function/tool calling from the console.
[00:32] Priya: thanks. so high level, redwood supports a JSON mode where you provide a schema and we try to return strictly-valid JSON, plus we have structured output guardrails that do entity extraction and validation. i'll share screen.
[00:44] [screen share starts]
[00:48] Priya: ok so here's the api request in the console, you can see schema field with a json schema, we set required fields: transaction_id, amount, currency, reason, recommended_action. when i run it you can see the model returns a json blob. sometimes the transcript that comes back from the model is slightly off, so we enforce schema at the runtime and optionally run a post-processor to coerce types or raise a schema error.
[01:12] Ethan: is the schema validation done client-side or on your infra?
[01:16] Priya: it's enforced on our side in the serving layer \u0004 we do a strict parse step. by default we try to coerce simple things (like numeric strings -> numbers) but you can opt in to strict mode which will return a structured error back. this keeps the downstream pipeline deterministic.
[01:30] Liam: what's the latency impact? coercion seems like extra work.
[01:34] Priya: good q \u0004 typical added time is ~10-40ms depending on payload size; most of the cost is model tokens. we showed microbenchmarks in the deck, and for our verified models it's within SLO for sub-200ms 95th on small payloads. if you go Dedicated you get more predictable p95.
[01:50] Maya: can you show the function calling part? we want to call an internal refund tool if the model recommends refund.
[01:56] Alex: sure \u0004 i'll switch to the tools demo. we have a feature where the model can emit a function call object, matching an allowed schema, and the runtime will either invoke your configured webhook or return the call object to the client. also we have guardrails to only allow whitelisted function names and parameter shapes.
[02:15] [Alex clicks around]
[02:18] Alex: here's a sample \u0004 model predicts recommended_action: "issue_refund" with params { transaction_id: "tx_123", amount: 45.00, reason: "duplicate charge" }. the console shows the function call, a preview of the payload, and audit trail. if you choose invoke, we POST to your webhook with HMAC signature and we log the invocation in the audit logs.
[02:38] Anika: about the webhook \u0004 what's the auth pattern?
[02:41] Alex: we support mutual TLS, HMAC signing, and you can deploy a private webhook inside your VPC via our Private offering with VPC NAT or direct peering. for hosted customers we recommend HMAC + retries + dead-letter queue.
[02:56] Ethan: are function calls replayable? we need idempotency keys for billing operations.
[03:00] Alex: yes the call payload includes an idempotency key. we also persist the call event and expose trace ids in the console so you can reconcile.
[03:10] Priya: one common pattern customers use is to have the model return a suggested action and then an obligate confirmation step from a service \u0004 so the model's output is advisory and your service performs the final authorization.
[03:25] Maya: ok that aligns with how we'd like to do it \u0004 model suggests refund, we run a fraud check pipeline, then issue refund.
[03:32] Liam: how do you handle hallucinations where model invents txn ids or amounts?
[03:36] Priya: two layers \u0004 schema enforcement to keep types and required fields, and runtime validation hooks where you can pass in a context of known transactions to constrain outputs. we also support retrieval-augmented prompts so the model can only reference known records. and we have a QA/regression tool in Redwood Optimize that will run your eval tests and alert on drift.
[03:58] Ethan: data residency \u0004 we process cardholder data; can Redwood guarantee logs don't leave region?
[04:03] James: with Private (VPC/on-prem) you control the data plane. for Dedicated we can provision capacity in-region and configure retention \u0004 we also offer field-level encryption and KMS integration; we support bringing-your-own-key (BYOK) and HSM integrations for enterprise plans.
[04:20] Anika: do you have SOC 2 and ISO certs?
[04:23] Priya: yes SOC 2 Type II in our security pack; i'll send the artifacts after the call. we also include audit logs, RBAC, and SSO (SAML/OIDC) integrations.
[04:33] Maya: in terms of cost, what's the delta for strict schema + function-calling flows?
[04:38] James: cost is mostly model compute; structured-output validation is a small add-on. for Hosted API it's usage-based; for Dedicated you get predictable unit costs and reserved capacity. i'll send a sample pricing sheet with expected per-1000-request unit cost for both modes.
[04:52] [15 minute mark in the demo, showing Console routing rules]
[04:55] Alex: another nice feature is smart routing \u0004 you can set a policy to route billing-critical requests to Dedicated or a lower-latency region and route exploratory requests to cheaper model variants. fallback policies ensure availability.
[05:12] Liam: can we do canary rollouts? we want to test model versions on a small percentage.
[05:15] Priya: yes, rollouts are supported in the console \u0004 canary, A/B, automatic rollback on quality regression. Redwood Optimize ties to your eval sets and will trigger alerts if JSON output metrics degrade.
[05:30] Ethan: for the pilot, what telemetry will we get? traces, token cost, per-route latency?
[05:34] James: yes \u0004 token-level cost, per-route p50/p95, per-model dashboards, and per-request trace ids which link to the raw transcript and structured output. we also expose logs to your SIEM via integrations.
[05:47] Maya: are there prebuilt prompts for disputes/billing?
[05:50] Priya: we have templates and an eval harness. most customers customize them but they speed up iteration.
[05:56] [small crosstalk \u0004 someone drops their mic briefly]
[06:05] Liam: real quick \u0004 if the schema fails, what's the failure mode? do you return raw text or an error code?
[06:10] Priya: depends on configuration: 1) relaxed: return coerced json (best-effort); 2) strict: return structured error with code and model raw output attached; 3) hybrid: emit a function call to a validation service before committing. all of these are logged.
[06:28] Ethan: how about security review turnaround? we have an internal security questionnaire.
[06:31] Priya: we typically answer standard questionnaires in 3-5 business days; for custom items we route to our security team \u0004 i'll put you in touch.
[06:38] Maya: demos look good. can you include an example of how the model's function call is sanitized so it can't call arbitrary endpoints?
[06:44] Alex: we whitelist function signatures and destination webhooks. the runtime will never call unregistered endpoints; we also support a allowlist of parameter values if you want extra safety.
[06:55] Anika: retention: how long do you keep audit logs and transcripts by default?
[06:59] James: default is 30 days for hosted, configurable up to enterprise tiers for longer retention; Dedicated and Private you can set retention policy or disable storage.
[07:10] Maya: what's next from our side if we want to pilot?
[07:13] Ethan: we'll need to confirm the scope, expected volume (we're thinking ~30k requests/day), and provide sample data for a 2-week pilot.
[07:20] James: great \u0004 so action items: i'll send pricing and a pilot template, priya will send security pack, you (Ethan) share sample traffic and liam share SLOs. we'll plan to kick off last week of september.
[07:32] Maya: sounds good. one more question \u0004 do you support streaming partial json responses for long contexts?
[07:36] Priya: yes we support streaming and chunked KV cache aware output; for structured output we stream JSON fragments but we always validate final payload. there are options to emit partial events with schema partials, but we recommend batching for long contexts.
[07:55] Ethan: any pitfalls with function calling and retries? we need to avoid double charges.
[07:59] Alex: retries include idempotency keys and we surface a retry trace; best practice is to handle dedupe on your side with idempotency and use webhook ack patterns we provide.
[08:12] [closing recap]
[08:15] James: recap: we'll send pricing + security pack, scope pilot for 30k/day, pilot template and kickoff next week.
[08:23] Maya: thanks all, looking forward.
[08:25] Anika: thanks.
[08:27] Ethan: bye.
